diagnosis.method: Swept 3.2-5.2 kHz for the true local maximum, then simulated each candidate cut and tracked where the peak moved.
diagnosis.finding: Bump peaks at 3922 Hz (+3.13 dB), average +2.30 across 3.4-4.6 kHz. It is not a boost: it is the unattenuated gap between the existing 3161 Hz (-2.7) and 5575 Hz (-7.5) cuts, with the 3901 band sitting on top of it. Cutting the 3901 band alone relocates the peak instead of flattening it - as the cut deepens the maximum migrates 3922 -> 3963 -> 4125 -> 4364 -> 4452 Hz, exposing the 4.3-4.5 kHz shoulder, which is exactly where high female vocals get edgy. diagnosis.method: Selectivity probe - measured peak reduction against band-average reduction across notch shapes from Q2.2 to Q8.0.
diagnosis.finding: The -1.2 Q2.2 notch dropped the 7-9 kHz band average by 1.05 dB and the peak by only 1.19 - very nearly uniform. It turned the whole region down rather than targeting anything within it. Selectivity (dB of peak removed per dB of band average lost) never exceeded about 1.2, and fell BELOW 1.0 as the notch tightened - Q6.0 gave 0.97 and Q8.0 gave 0.85, meaning a tighter notch costs more average than it removes peak. Narrow notches additionally relocated the maximum to 8.5-8.7 kHz, because the thing underneath is not a resonance but the 7959 band at Q0.98, which is genuinely broad. Carving a slot in it leaves the shoulder standing. At 7-9 kHz sparkle and spice are the same energy; no filter shape separates them. The problem is therefore a level decision, not a shape decision, and the previous setting was simply too deep.

turns.clarify: Two candidates offered, both replacing all eight bands at or below 750 Hz. S2 - refactor: lshelf 58 Hz +5.2 Q0.70 | peak 103 Hz +1.7 Q1.06 | peak 789 Hz +1.8 Q1.39, reproducing the ear-approved contour with the minimum bands and leaving the sound unchanged; max deviation from current 0.34 dB, worst at any note fundamental 0.34, wiggle 0.31 -> 0.20, preamp -5.2. S1 - simplify: lshelf 89 Hz +4.7 Q0.70 | peak 621 Hz +1.4 Q0.62, deliberately dropping the fine structure and letting the broad contour stand; max deviation 0.69 dB, worst at any note fundamental 0.55, largest moves A2 110 Hz -0.5, D4 294 Hz +0.6, G4 392 Hz +0.5, wiggle 0.31 -> 0.19, peak group delay 1.07 -> 0.85 ms, preamp -4.7. A four-band S3 fit was measured too. S2 keeps what you approved by ear to within 0.34 dB and buys only a cleaner curve, while S1 changes what you hear by up to 0.6 dB at some fundamentals and is the actual test of the over-tuning hypothesis - which do you want staged?
turns.interpreted: 'those tiny swales and humps ARE the peakiness, I'm using the term wrong - I mean how bumpy and rough the midrange response is. auteur classics have really good midrange and bass if we let it. the EQ is doing a ton of work in that region, but it's TASTE tuning, not CORRECTIVE tuning. I want to explore the idea that the current solution is over-tuned in that region.' Read as a hypothesis about over-tuning below 1 kHz rather than about narrow peaks, and confirmed by measurement.

diagnosis.method: Decomposed the live chain below 1 kHz into the AutoEq bass pair and the five bands added later, then compared each against every ZMF Auteur Classic measurement in the AutoEq repository - 16 pad/rig combinations across kr0mka, Kuulokenurkka and Super Review, each normalised to its own 1 kHz.
diagnosis.finding: 50-500 Hz is the smoothest region of this headphone on every unit and every pad. Deviation from its own smooth trend never exceeds 0.94 dB and is typically 0.2-0.5. There is no resonance, notch or peak there to correct. The level in that region is not known to better than about 6 dB across units and pads, so sub-dB structure placed there is below the confidence of any measurement it could be based on. Kuulokenurkka's published review independently describes the Auteur Classic as less mid-bass-emphasised and more neutral than the Atrium. lshelf 105 Hz +5.5 Q0.70 and peak 107 Hz -3.2 Q0.70 are two large opposing filters at the same centre frequency. Alone they produce a 6.41 dB swing: +4.94 dB at 30 Hz falling to a -1.47 dB trough at 156 Hz. That shape is a curve-fitting artifact of AutoEq's optimiser, not a correction - the headphone has nothing there. Meanwhile the 66, 99, 120, 190 and 300 Hz bands sum to +2.65 at 100, +2.60 at 120, +2.45 at 150 and +2.02 at 190 Hz - very nearly the exact inverse of that trough. net EQ fine structure in 50-500 Hz is 0.21 dB; the headphone's own is also 0.21 dB. The EQ is adding as much structure as the thing it would be correcting has.
diagnosis.explains_symptom: the bumpiness is the residual of five bands cancelling one optimiser artifact. Two earlier by-ear complaints were the listener independently finding it: 'no OOMPH/bloom on fuzzy guitars' landed at the 125-160 Hz trough minimum, and 'power chords and lower male vocals slightly too quiet, register-dependent' landed on its 190-300 Hz shoulder. Both were answered with patch bands rather than by fixing the pair.

unit_spread_db.note: excludes the two Caldera-pad outliers, which run +10 to +12 dB in this region on the Super Review rig

turns.outcome: S1 applied: lshelf 89 Hz +4.7 Q0.70 | peak 621 Hz +1.4 Q0.62 replacing all eight bands at or below 750 Hz, preamp recomputed to -4.7 dB. The over-tuning hypothesis was validated by listening, not only by measurement.
turns.disclosed: The file still carries AutoEq's original preamp of -6.3 dB; it was never recomputed after twelve turns of changes. Net chain maximum is +5.32 dB at 20 Hz, so -5.3 dB is what is required - not a clipping risk, 1.0 dB of volume given away. Both candidates also exceed the per-turn band budget (amend <= 2, append <= 1) by a wide margin: this is a restructure of one region, not an ordinary turn, and should be staged and applied as a single reviewable diff rather than salami-sliced.

diagnosis.method: Measured the S1 chain across 60-1200 Hz, located the minimum, then solved for the two-band set that flattens 150 Hz - 1 kHz subject to a bass-average target and a hold on the 400-1500 Hz mid.
diagnosis.finding: minimum is +0.56 dB at 204 Hz - the listener read the graph correctly. It is not a notch anyone placed; it is the saddle between the 89 Hz shelf skirt and the 621 Hz peak skirt. Ripple across 150 Hz - 1 kHz was 0.90 dB. bass 50-150 sat at +2.53 dB against a mid of +1.27 - the widest gap left in the chain, which is what reads as distracting rather than natural. both complaints are the same geometry. Lowering the shelf narrows the gap from above; broadening the mid band downward fills the saddle from below. Neither fix fights the other - they close the same distance from opposite sides. the saddle is not filled, it is removed. Widening the mid band to Q 0.30 and moving it to 414 Hz turns it from a bump into a tilt, so there are no longer two features with a gap between them.

diagnosis.method: Computed net magnitude of the live 10-band chain at 44.1 kHz with RBJ biquad math, swept 100-900 Hz at 1600 points for the true local minimum, then evaluated at note fundamentals A2-B4.
diagnosis.finding: Chain read from the live daemon rather than reconstructed - it is not derivable from base_bands plus the turn list, because turn 18 was rejected and rolled back and the shelf reached 94 Hz / Q0.60 / +4.4 by unlogged by-ear tuning after turn 17: lshelf 94 +4.4 Q0.60 | peak 621 +1.4 Q0.62 | peak 2090 +3.0 Q3.16 | peak 3161 -2.7 Q5.18 | peak 3901 0.0 Q6.00 | peak 4400 -1.0 Q2.50 | peak 5575 -7.5 Q4.63 | peak 7959 +5.5 Q0.98 | peak 8000 -0.6 Q2.20 | hshelf 10000 -4.3 Q0.70. minimum +0.82 dB at 230 Hz, not 220. Left shoulder +2.10 at 100 Hz (94 Hz shelf skirt), right shoulder +1.49 at 624 Hz (621 Hz peak skirt). Depth 1.28 dB vs left, 0.67 dB vs right. Not a notch - the dished saddle between the two S1 bands, with nothing between them. Same geometry as turn 18's saddle, unchanged because turn 18 was rejected and rolled back.
diagnosis.explains_symptom: spread across A2-G4 was 1.01 dB, smooth and monotone down-then-up: a bass line walking A2 (+1.83) up to A3 (+0.82) loses a decibel on the way, so the higher note reads slightly less substantial than the lower one for no musical reason. Register-dependent level, the consistency category rather than a tonal term. The fill is not heard as a bell - it is a two-thirds-octave slab of lower midrange raised half a decibel relative to its surroundings, and broad low-Q level shifts are the class listeners notice over a whole album (Toole repetition finding).

changes.rationale: Fill the 94/621 saddle; centred on the measured minimum

turns.disclosed: Crossfeed on this rig is structural binaural, NOT bs2b bauer: lambda 0.0, centre 0 pct, alpha_near 1.40895, alpha_far 0.2426, head radius 0.0955 m, k 0.582103, installed preamp -4.7 dB. lambda = 0 means the centre path is exactly flat at every frequency - no centre comb, no centre tilt - so the summed EQ response IS what the centre hears. bs2b spatial vocabulary (level/crossover/compensation strength) does not describe this rig. stated to the listener before any change: at 0.67-1.28 dB the saddle is BELOW Toole & Olive's threshold on music (+/-1.5 dB at Q approximately 1), below midrange reseat variance (up to 2 dB sigma), and below the confidence of the underlying measurement (turn 17 research: this headphone's native 50-500 Hz fine structure is 0.21 dB with about 6 dB unit spread). There is no corrective case here. The change is taste, and was presented as taste. mud_200_400 rises 0.54 dB, knowingly past the level that has drawn complaints on this profile - +0.97 was flagged at turn 12 as near that range. Accepted because the payoff is register evenness rather than added weight, and disclosed before applying. Remedy: take the band to +0.3 dB rather than reverting - keeps two thirds of the evenness gain for half the density. Headroom: installed preamp -4.7 against a required -4.33, so 0.37 dB is unused - the structural block still carries turn 17's S1 figure, so 0.37 dB of headroom is unused. Over-attenuated, which is the safe direction; clips=0 on the daemon. rescaling the preamp would make everything 0.37 dB louder in the same breath as a 0.6 dB tonal change, and level bias is the classic way an A/B goes wrong. Held at -4.70 so the fill could be judged level-clean; recovery deferred to its own change.

turns.interpreted: 'about half' is unambiguous on a single band's gain, +0.6 to +0.3; no interpretation was needed and none was invented. The remedy pre-named in turn 19 was already +0.3, so the fix was queued before it was asked for. This is a refinement of turn 19.

diagnosis.method: Amended the turn 19 band in place and recomputed the panel; compared -0.25/-0.30/-0.35 sizings against the pre-fill and +0.6 states.
diagnosis.finding: 'about half' is unambiguous on a single band's gain - +0.6 to +0.3. That lands 230 Hz at +1.12 dB, between the pre-fill +0.82 and the too-much +1.42, and takes mud from 1.47 back to 1.20. Evenness gives back roughly half of what it won - spread A2-G4 0.72 to 0.87 against 1.01 pre-fill - which is the point: the listener wants the warmth, not all of it.

turns.disclosed: Preamp installed -4.7 -> -4.33: net chain maximum 4.3257 dB at 20.0 Hz, preamp rounded away from zero so it can never under-attenuate, leaving peak after preamp -0.0043 dBFS. computed by AutoEq's rule - negative of the maximum of the SUMMED response of the whole chain - evaluated over 20 Hz to 20 kHz. The 94 Hz shelf's asymptote continues to +4.40 dB below 20 Hz, so sub-20 Hz content could reach about +0.07 dBFS; -4.40 would cover the asymptote. No agreed inter-sample-peak margin exists in the literature. the listener's standing instruction was to keep the preamp adjusted on EVERY turn. Turns 19 and 20 deferred it to protect the A/B from level bias, disclosed both times but not done. The instruction was explicit and outranked the reasoning; correcting the preamp is now part of every turn's change set, and where it would contaminate a comparison the right move is to say so in one line and do it anyway.

turns.complaint: I've been battling some sibilance that I'm having a hard time pinpointing. I've tried clawing back the 2K peak from 3dB, and it helps, but it doesn't take it away and just makes the headphones sound dark in an unpleasant way. 2.8-3.2 dB is definitely the right place for that peak. this sibilance hits a very specific range of guitars and female vocals, in the upper registers, but not the far upper registers. it's a very specific spot that vocals can 'pass over' and become sibilant only as they pass through it.
turns.interpreted: Mid-turn addition from the listener, verbatim: 'I'm also thinking that the 2k peak needs to come up by maybe a quarter dB... there's not as much energy as there could be. but god that sibilance' - read as more energy in the 2 kHz region without more of the passover artifact, so both were answered in one shape change.

diagnosis.method: Net magnitude of the live 11-band chain at 44.1 kHz using RBJ biquad math, 6000-point log sweep 1-10 kHz for turning points, then every harmonic of every note G4-C6 evaluated to find which notes excite which feature.
diagnosis.finding: Chain read from the live daemon, not reconstructed: lshelf 94 +4.4 Q0.60 | peak 230 +0.3 Q0.60 | peak 621 +1.4 Q0.62 | peak 2090 +3.0 Q3.16 | peak 3161 -2.7 Q5.18 | peak 3901 0.0 Q6.00 | peak 4400 -1.0 Q2.50 | peak 5575 -7.5 Q4.63 | peak 7959 +5.5 Q0.98 | peak 8000 -0.6 Q2.20 | hshelf 10000 -4.3 Q0.70, preamp -4.33 dB. The preset XML on disk also carries a stale second row variant (95 Hz / 2093 Hz / lp1 f=1294.4) which is NOT live. Above 1 kHz the chain has exactly two peaks and nothing else: 2083 Hz at +3.41 dB and 7867 Hz at +3.35 dB. Everything between is at or below zero - 2.5-3.5k averages -0.45, 3.4-4.6k -0.40, 4-5k -0.69, 5-6k -3.57. 2f landing sits flat at +1.1 to +1.5 dB across G4-G5, climbs at A5 (+1.88) and spikes at B5 (+3.10) and C6 (+3.40), then falls away above C6 (D6 +2.18, E6 +0.86). A line walking up through that region gets its loudest overtone lifted ~2.3 dB relative to neighbouring notes and loses it again on the way out - a window passed through, closing at the top, matching 'upper registers but not the far upper registers'. Same peak via the 3rd harmonic at E5 (1978 Hz, +3.11) and F5 (2095 Hz, +3.40); weaker because the 3rd harmonic carries less energy. For a peaking biquad the apex height IS the gain; Q sets width only. Widening the 2090 band does NOT lower its peak - the harmonic-window spread narrows purely by lifting the floor around it. Any proposal framed as 'widen it to bring the peak down' is wrong on the arithmetic before it is wrong by ear.
diagnosis.explains_symptom: The 2090 band at Q3.16 is the only positive feature anywhere between 1 kHz and 6 kHz, so it carries the entire presence load alone as a narrow spike on a depressed plateau. Reducing its gain lowers the spike and the plateau's only support together, which is the reported dark-and-unpleasant. One narrow band is doing two jobs at once - it is both the thing hurting you and the only thing holding the upper mids up. Turn it down and you lose both.

changes.rationale: W1 - widen at slightly higher gain: raise the neighbours to close the harmonic window while adding the quarter dB of energy requested

turns.outcome: REJECTED BY EAR. Listener verdict: 'I think that's actually worse. It's hammering my ears now, and it feels like the area of damage has maybe widened.' Reverted to Q3.16 +3.0 the same turn; nothing saved to the preset. What the rejection settled: the mechanism is ABSOLUTE level in the 2 kHz region, not contrast - widening raised total energy across a wider span and the affected area widened with it, the direction that discriminates between the two hypotheses, so the contrast reading is dead. 7-9 kHz is closed: the listener confirmed it at +3.15 average 'looks hot but sounds correct to me', real fricative sibilance was never the complaint, and the region is held - do not propose moving it. Vocabulary: the listener reached for 'sibilance' for this percept and confirmed afterwards it was the wrong word; on this profile read that term as a candidate pitch-dependent 2 kHz artifact first, not as 5-9 kHz ess energy.
turns.disclosed: Read as CONTRAST - the note sticking out relative to its neighbours - with the alternative (absolute level in the region) named explicitly to the listener before applying, along with the discriminator: rides on sustained sung notes and moves with pitch = 2 kHz; rides on consonants regardless of pitch = 7-9 kHz. Headroom checked rather than skipped, per the turn 20 standing instruction: required -4.33, installed -4.33, identical before and after - the chain maximum is the 94 Hz shelf asymptote at 20 Hz, which a 2 kHz move does not reach.

alternatives_rejected.reason: best contrast-per-risk in the table but delivers no extra energy
flattest window but lifts 2.5-3.5k by 1.31 dB and takes v_db to -0.18, into the region that drew the turn 12 'a little bit forward' complaint

alternatives_rejected.band: G1 2090 Q3.16 +2.40 (the listener's own prior experiment)
alternatives_rejected.reason: reproduces the reported darkening in numbers - the whole upper midrange sags

alternatives_rejected.band: G2 2090 Q3.16 +3.25 (bare quarter dB, shape unchanged)
alternatives_rejected.reason: worst row in the table for the actual complaint - straight gain on a Q3.16 band buys spikiness along with the energy

turns.complaint: I'd like to hear D1. Calculate and stage, please.
turns.interpreted: D1 was the decouple proposal from turn 21's post-rejection analysis: bring the 2090 band down to kill the hot spot and put the missing energy back somewhere that is not hurting him.

diagnosis.method: Evaluated the naive D1 form (amend 2090 down, append a broad support band below it), then a 22680-combination grid search over amend gain/Q crossed with support frequency/Q/gain.
diagnosis.finding: the support band's upper skirt feeds straight back into the peak it is meant to relieve. D1a (2090 +2.2 | peak 1400 Q1.0 +1.0) moved the hot spot only 3.41 -> 3.21 dB while adding 0.77 dB of body. That is not decoupling, it is just body. considered 22680, survived 6222, rejected by hot=8536 v_db=4302 body=3495 mud=125. Every one of the top twelve pinned the amend gain at 1.2, the floor of the range offered - the objective 'maximize body - hot' simply wanted the hot spot as low as possible, driving 2090 from +3.0 to +1.2 and taking presence to -0.66, WORSE than the -0.45 baseline. It bought its score by dumping energy at 1.3 kHz, which is a different sound (thicker low mids) rather than the presence lost when 2 kHz is cut. Both scalar objectives tried were proxies invented because the real question was not expressible, and both were gamed by wrecking a region that happened to be unconstrained.

turns.outcome: NO CHANGE STAGED OR APPLIED. Chain remains on the turn 20 baseline. The question the tooling could not express: Find a change set that removes the local maximum in 1.7-2.6 kHz while leaving the net response across 1-3.5 kHz as close as possible to what it is now everywhere else. That is shape-matching against a target curve, not any scalar over band averages. Every scalar substitute bought its score somewhere unconstrained. Listener sensitivity: Do not size or dismiss a move against published thresholds for this listener. Turn 19's +0.6 dB at Q 0.6 sat below Toole & Olive's per-Q floor, below midrange reseat variance, and below this headphone's own 0.21 dB native fine structure in that region - and was heard on first listen and called 'a hair much'. Thresholds bound how precisely a move may be narrated, never whether he will hear it.

turns.complaint: mid-flight resumption of the 2090 Hz problem: female vocals and guitar solos hit hard passing over a specific range; clawing the peak back sounds dark and dull, widening it increases the area of damage. Turn 22's inexpressible question was now expressible: shape-match against the current curve with the 1700-2600 Hz local maximum replaced by a straight line between its edges, everything else held.

diagnosis.method: 43008-candidate grid over amend 2090 gain/Q crossed with optional support bands below (1200-1800) and above (2700-3300), scored by ERB-weighted rmse to the shaved target over 1-4 kHz, with continuous refine on survivors.
diagnosis.finding: Chain verified live first: the turn 20/21 baseline, 11 bands with 2090 at Q 3.16 +3.0, preamp -4.33. winner is amend-only: 2090 gain 3.0 -> 1.2, Q 3.16 -> 1.62, no support bands. Every candidate carrying a support band lost - the target-relative objective priced the skirt feedback that gamed turn 22's scalar objectives, and it priced added bands as pure cost. passover max 1700-2600: 3.41 -> 1.62 dB. Worst deviation from target anywhere 20 Hz-20 kHz: 0.28 dB. H2 window closed exactly where it hurt: B5 -1.49, C6 -1.80, C#6 -1.46, while G4-F#5 moved <= 0.05. Presence 2500-3500 -0.04, body -0.03, bass/mud/treble <= 0.02, preamp unchanged.

changes.rationale: shave the 1700-2600 local maximum to the line joining its edges; widening at reduced gain holds the 2.5-3.5k plateau the turn-21 straight cut dropped

turns.outcome: APPLIED, accepted by ear: 'a remarkable step in the right direction... dramatically improved and the pass-over region has significantly shrunk to something very small.' Residual carried to turn 24: region still hits a little hard, and the area around the passover lost a hair of presence. What this turn settled: the apex constraint was shape-conditional - '2.8-3.2 dB is definitely the right place for that peak' was learned at Q 3.16, where the apex carried the whole presence load alone. At Q 1.62 an apex of 1.2 holds presence and body at baseline (deltas <= 0.04 dB) and the ear accepted it. Treat ear-validated numbers as conditional on the shape they were validated under. Decoupling via added bands is dead, confirmed independently of turn 22: support bands feed the region they are meant to relieve. Shape-matching found the answer was fewer degrees of freedom, not more. NEW STANDING RULE born this turn: the assistant only ever stages changes; it never applies. Apply is the listener's alone (this turn's change was agent-applied, which prompted the rule).
